Differentiation asks: given a function, how fast is it changing? This unit asks the opposite question: given the rate of change, what was the function? The answer is called an anti-derivative, and the process of finding it is integration. Eighteen teaching hours make this the largest single unit in Grade 12 Mathematics, and it is also the one that pays best in the examination: Group B always carries integration items and Group C almost always carries one. The same machinery then measures areas, and in the next unit it solves differential equations.

What the exam asks

Three things, in this order of frequency. (1) Evaluate an indefinite integral — you must recognise which of about a dozen methods applies. (2) Evaluate a definite integral, often using a symmetry property to avoid work. (3) Find an area, or evaluate an integral as the limit of a sum. Students lose marks by choosing the wrong method, not by mis-executing the right one, so learn the decision table in §13.2 before you learn any single technique.

13.1 Standard integrals

The anti-derivative and the indefinite integral

Anti-derivative

A function F is an anti-derivative of f on an interval if F'(x) = f(x) for every x in that interval.

If F is one anti-derivative of f, then so is F(x) + C for every constant C, because the derivative of a constant is zero. Conversely, any two anti-derivatives of the same function differ by a constant. The whole family is written

\int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C

and is called the indefinite integral of f. Here f(x) is the integrand, x is the variable of integration, and C is the constant of integration.

Why must two anti-derivatives differ only by a constant? If F' = G' = f, then (F-G)' = 0 everywhere, and a function with zero derivative on an interval is constant. So the picture of an indefinite integral is a vertical stack of identical curves: at any fixed x every member of the stack has exactly the same slope.

The table you must know by heart

Every integration problem in the syllabus ends by matching something to a line of this table. Learn it by reading each line backwards as a derivative.

\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} - \frac{a^{2}}{2}\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\right| + C

The last nine lines are the quadratic standard forms. Roughly half of all Group B integration questions reduce to one of them.

Two rules let you use the table on a whole expression at once. For constants k and integrable f, g:

\int k\,f(x)\,dx = k\int f(x)\,dx, \qquad \int \left[f(x) \pm g(x)\right]dx = \int f(x)\,dx \pm \int g(x)\,dx

There is no product rule and no quotient rule for integrals. That missing pair of rules is the reason this unit needs so many separate methods.

Because of that, integration is a recognition skill rather than a procedure. Differentiation can be done mechanically by anyone who knows three rules, but integration asks you to look at an expression and decide what it is disguised as. That is why practice matters more here than anywhere else in the syllabus, and why the first thing to do with any integral is not to start writing but to spend ten seconds classifying it.

A third rule follows from the chain rule and costs nothing to learn. If \int f(x)\,dx = F(x) + C then, for constants a \ne 0 and b,

\int f(ax+b)\,dx = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) + C

because differentiating the right side brings a factor a down, which cancels the \frac{1}{a}.

Worked example 13.1

Problem. Evaluate \int \left(3x^{2} - \frac{4}{x} + 5\sqrt{x} + e^{x}\right)dx.

Solution. Split the integral term by term and apply the table to each.

\int 3x^{2}\,dx = 3\cdot\frac{x^{3}}{3} = x^{3}

\int \frac{4}{x}\,dx = 4\ln|x|

For 5\sqrt{x} = 5x^{1/2} the power rule gives exponent \frac12 + 1 = \frac32:

\int 5x^{1/2}\,dx = 5\cdot\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2} = \frac{10}{3}x^{3/2}

and \int e^{x}dx = e^{x}. Collecting, and writing one constant for all four,

\int \left(3x^{2} - \frac{4}{x} + 5\sqrt{x} + e^{x}\right)dx = x^{3} - 4\ln|x| + \frac{10}{3}x^{3/2} + e^{x} + C

Check. Differentiate: 3x^{2} - \frac4x + \frac{10}{3}\cdot\frac32 x^{1/2} + e^{x} = 3x^{2} - \frac4x + 5\sqrt{x} + e^{x}. Correct.

Worked example 13.2

Problem. Evaluate \int \left(\sqrt{x} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^{2}dx and \int \frac{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}{x^{2}}\,dx.

Solution. Neither integrand is in the table, but both become table entries after ordinary algebra. Always expand or divide out first.

\left(\sqrt{x} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\right)^{2} = x + 2 + \frac{1}{x}

\int \left(x + 2 + \frac1x\right)dx = \frac{x^{2}}{2} + 2x + \ln|x| + C

For the second, expand the numerator and divide each term by x^{2}:

\frac{x^{4} + 2x^{2} + 1}{x^{2}} = x^{2} + 2 + x^{-2}

\int \left(x^{2} + 2 + x^{-2}\right)dx = \frac{x^{3}}{3} + 2x - \frac{1}{x} + C

Worked example 13.3

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int \tan^{2}x\,dx, (b) \int \sin^{2}x\,dx, (c) \int \frac{dx}{1+\cos x}.

Solution. Every one of these is solved by a trigonometric identity, not by a new integration rule.

(a) Use \sec^{2}x - \tan^{2}x = 1, so \tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1:

\int \tan^{2}x\,dx = \int \left(\sec^{2}x - 1\right)dx = \tan x - x + C

(b) Use the power-reduction identity \cos 2x = 1 - 2\sin^{2}x, so \sin^{2}x = \frac{1 - \cos 2x}{2}:

\int \sin^{2}x\,dx = \frac12\int (1 - \cos 2x)\,dx = \frac{x}{2} - \frac{\sin 2x}{4} + C

(c) Use 1 + \cos x = 2\cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}:

\int \frac{dx}{2\cos^{2}\frac{x}{2}} = \frac12\int \sec^{2}\frac{x}{2}\,dx = \frac12 \cdot \frac{\tan\frac{x}{2}}{1/2} + C = \tan\frac{x}{2} + C

Worked example 13.4

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int (2x+3)^{5}dx, (b) \int \frac{dx}{3x+2}, (c) \int \sin(5x-2)\,dx, (d) \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x+1}}.

Solution. All four are of the form f(ax+b), so integrate as if the bracket were x and divide by a.

(a) a = 2: \quad \int (2x+3)^{5}dx = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{(2x+3)^{6}}{6} + C = \frac{(2x+3)^{6}}{12} + C

(b) a = 3: \quad \int \frac{dx}{3x+2} = \frac{1}{3}\ln|3x+2| + C

(c) a = 5: \quad \int \sin(5x-2)\,dx = -\frac{1}{5}\cos(5x-2) + C

(d) a = 2 and \int x^{-1/2}dx = 2\sqrt{x}: \quad \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{2x+1}} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\sqrt{2x+1} + C = \sqrt{2x+1} + C

The rule \int f(ax+b) = \frac{1}{a}F(ax+b) needs ax+b **linear**

It works for (2x+3)^{5} but not for (2x^{2}+3)^{5}, because differentiating (2x^{2}+3)^{6} produces 4x, not a constant. A non-linear inside function always needs a substitution, and the substitution only closes if the derivative of the inside function is already present as a factor.

Never drop the +C

An indefinite integral without +C is one function instead of a whole family, and NEB markers deduct for it every single time. Also remember \ln|x|, not \ln x: the modulus is what makes the formula valid for negative x too.

13.2 Integrals reducible to standard forms

Most integrands are not in the table. The art is to change them into something that is. Read this decision table first; then learn the individual techniques.

Read the table from the top down and stop at the first row that fits. The rows are deliberately in that order: the cheap checks — is it already standard, can it be expanded, is it linear inside — come before the expensive ones. A great many marks are thrown away each year by students who reach for integration by parts on an integral that a single substitution would have finished in two lines, or who attempt partial fractions on a fraction that is not yet proper.

Integration by substitution

If we put u = g(x) then du = g'(x)\,dx, and

\int f\left(g(x)\right)g'(x)\,dx = \int f(u)\,du

The substitution closes only when every remaining x disappears. That is the test: after substituting, if any x is left, the choice of u was wrong.

Worked example 13.5

Problem. Evaluate \int x\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\,dx.

Solution. The derivative of x^{2}+1 is 2x, and an x is already present.

Put u = x^{2}+1, so du = 2x\,dx, i.e. x\,dx = \frac{du}{2}.

\int x\sqrt{x^{2}+1}\,dx = \int \sqrt{u}\,\frac{du}{2} = \frac12 \cdot \frac{u^{3/2}}{3/2} = \frac{u^{3/2}}{3}

Put u back: \quad = \frac{1}{3}\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{3/2} + C.

Check. \frac{d}{dx}\frac{(x^{2}+1)^{3/2}}{3} = \frac{1}{3}\cdot\frac32(x^{2}+1)^{1/2}\cdot 2x = x\sqrt{x^{2}+1}. Correct.

The single most useful substitution

\int \frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\,dx = \ln|g(x)| + C

Whenever the numerator is exactly the derivative of the denominator (or a constant times it), write down the logarithm immediately. This one pattern produces \int\tan x\,dx, \int\cot x\,dx, \int\frac{x^{3}}{x^{4}+5}dx and half of every partial-fraction answer.

Worked example 13.6

Problem. Prove that \int \tan x\,dx = \ln|\sec x| + C and \int \cot x\,dx = \ln|\sin x| + C.

Solution. Write \tan x = \dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} and put u = \cos x, so du = -\sin x\,dx:

\int \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}\,dx = -\int \frac{du}{u} = -\ln|u| + C = -\ln|\cos x| + C = \ln\left|\frac{1}{\cos x}\right| + C = \ln|\sec x| + C

For the cotangent, u = \sin x gives du = \cos x\,dx and the numerator is already \cos x:

\int \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\,dx = \int \frac{du}{u} = \ln|\sin x| + C

Worked example 13.7

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int \frac{e^{\tan^{-1}x}}{1+x^{2}}\,dx, (b) \int \frac{x^{3}}{x^{4}+5}\,dx, (c) \int \frac{dx}{x\ln x}, (d) \int \sin^{3}x\cos x\,dx.

Solution. In each case spot the inside function and its derivative.

(a) u = \tan^{-1}x, du = \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}}: \quad \int e^{u}du = e^{u} + C = e^{\tan^{-1}x} + C

(b) u = x^{4}+5, du = 4x^{3}dx: \quad \frac14\int\frac{du}{u} = \frac14\ln\left|x^{4}+5\right| + C

(c) u = \ln x, du = \frac{dx}{x}: \quad \int\frac{du}{u} = \ln\left|\ln x\right| + C

(d) u = \sin x, du = \cos x\,dx: \quad \int u^{3}du = \frac{u^{4}}{4} + C = \frac{\sin^{4}x}{4} + C

Worked example 13.8

Problem. Prove the standard result \int \sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C.

Solution. The trick is to multiply and divide by \sec x + \tan x, which manufactures a "derivative over function" pattern.

\int \sec x\,dx = \int \sec x \cdot \frac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx = \int \frac{\sec^{2}x + \sec x\tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}\,dx

Now put u = \sec x + \tan x. Then du = \left(\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x\right)dx, which is exactly the numerator:

\int \frac{du}{u} = \ln|u| + C = \ln\left|\sec x + \tan x\right| + C

The same trick with \csc x - \cot x gives \int \csc x\,dx = \ln|\csc x - \cot x| + C.

Integration by parts

The formula for integration by parts

Start from the product rule for two differentiable functions u and v:

\frac{d}{dx}(uv) = u\frac{dv}{dx} + v\frac{du}{dx}

Integrate both sides with respect to x. The left side integrates back to uv:

uv = \int u\frac{dv}{dx}\,dx + \int v\frac{du}{dx}\,dx

Rearranging gives the working formula

\int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du

or, with u = u(x) and dv = v'(x)\,dx written out in full,

\int u(x)\,v'(x)\,dx = u(x)v(x) - \int v(x)\,u'(x)\,dx

The method is useful exactly when \int v\,du is easier than \int u\,dv.

ILATE — which factor to call u

Choose u as the function that comes first in this list:

I — Inverse trigonometric (\sin^{-1}x, \tan^{-1}x, …) L — Logarithmic (\ln x) A — Algebraic (x, x^{2}, polynomials) T — Trigonometric (\sin x, \cos x) E — Exponential (e^{x}, a^{x})

The rest of the integrand is dv. The logic is that I and L get simpler when differentiated, while T and E are just as easy to integrate as to differentiate.

Worked example 13.9

Problem. Evaluate \int x e^{x}\,dx.

Solution. Algebraic before Exponential, so u = x and dv = e^{x}dx.

Then du = dx and v = e^{x}.

\int x e^{x}dx = x e^{x} - \int e^{x}\,dx = x e^{x} - e^{x} + C = (x-1)e^{x} + C

Check. \frac{d}{dx}\left[(x-1)e^{x}\right] = e^{x} + (x-1)e^{x} = x e^{x}. Correct.

Had we chosen u = e^{x} instead, we would have got \frac{x^{2}}{2}e^{x} - \int \frac{x^{2}}{2}e^{x}dx — a harder integral. That is what ILATE protects you from.

Worked example 13.10

Problem. Evaluate \int x^{2}\sin x\,dx (the repeated case).

Solution. Algebraic before Trigonometric: u = x^{2}, dv = \sin x\,dx, so du = 2x\,dx and v = -\cos x.

\int x^{2}\sin x\,dx = -x^{2}\cos x + 2\int x\cos x\,dx

The new integral is still a product, but the power of x has dropped by one. Apply parts again with u = x, dv = \cos x\,dx, v = \sin x:

\int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x - \int \sin x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x

Substituting back,

\int x^{2}\sin x\,dx = -x^{2}\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C

Check. Differentiating gives -2x\cos x + x^{2}\sin x + 2\sin x + 2x\cos x - 2\sin x = x^{2}\sin x. Correct. An integrand x^{n}\sin x needs exactly n applications of parts.

Worked example 13.11

Problem. Evaluate \int \ln x\,dx, \int x^{2}\ln x\,dx and \int \tan^{-1}x\,dx.

Solution. A lone logarithm or inverse-trig function is integrated against the invisible factor 1.

(a) u = \ln x, dv = 1\,dx, so du = \frac{dx}{x} and v = x:

\int \ln x\,dx = x\ln x - \int x\cdot\frac{1}{x}\,dx = x\ln x - x + C

(b) L before A: u = \ln x, dv = x^{2}dx, so v = \frac{x^{3}}{3}:

\int x^{2}\ln x\,dx = \frac{x^{3}}{3}\ln x - \int \frac{x^{3}}{3}\cdot\frac1x\,dx = \frac{x^{3}}{3}\ln x - \frac{x^{3}}{9} + C

(c) u = \tan^{-1}x, dv = 1\,dx, so du = \frac{dx}{1+x^{2}} and v = x:

\int \tan^{-1}x\,dx = x\tan^{-1}x - \int \frac{x}{1+x^{2}}\,dx = x\tan^{-1}x - \frac12\ln\left(1+x^{2}\right) + C

using \int\frac{g'}{g} = \ln|g| with g = 1+x^{2} (always positive, so no modulus is needed).

Worked example 13.12

Problem. Evaluate I = \int e^{x}\sin x\,dx (the cyclic case).

Solution. Neither factor simplifies on differentiation, so parts will never terminate. Instead, apply it twice and recover the original integral.

Take u = \sin x, dv = e^{x}dx, so v = e^{x}:

I = e^{x}\sin x - \int e^{x}\cos x\,dx

Apply parts to the new integral with u = \cos x, dv = e^{x}dx:

\int e^{x}\cos x\,dx = e^{x}\cos x + \int e^{x}\sin x\,dx = e^{x}\cos x + I

Substituting back,

I = e^{x}\sin x - e^{x}\cos x - I \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2I = e^{x}(\sin x - \cos x)

I = \frac{e^{x}}{2}\left(\sin x - \cos x\right) + C

The general result, obtained the same way, is

\int e^{ax}\cos bx\,dx = \frac{e^{ax}}{a^{2}+b^{2}}\left(a\cos bx + b\sin bx\right) + C

For example \int e^{2x}\cos 3x\,dx = \frac{e^{2x}}{13}\left(2\cos 3x + 3\sin 3x\right) + C.

The \int e^{x}\left[f(x)+f'(x)\right]dx shortcut

\int e^{x}\left[f(x) + f'(x)\right]dx = e^{x}f(x) + C

Proof: differentiate the right side. So \int e^{x}(\sin x + \cos x)\,dx = e^{x}\sin x + C in one line. Look for this pattern before doing parts twice — it saves several minutes in the examination.

Reducing to the quadratic standard forms

\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}-a^{2}} and \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}}

First form. Split by partial fractions, using \frac{1}{x^{2}-a^{2}} = \frac{1}{(x-a)(x+a)} and the identity \frac{1}{(x-a)(x+a)} = \frac{1}{2a}\left[\frac{1}{x-a} - \frac{1}{x+a}\right]:

\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}-a^{2}} = \frac{1}{2a}\left[\ln|x-a| - \ln|x+a|\right] + C = \frac{1}{2a}\ln\left|\frac{x-a}{x+a}\right| + C

Second form. Put x = a\tan\theta, so dx = a\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta and \sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}} = a\sec\theta:

\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}} = \int \frac{a\sec^{2}\theta}{a\sec\theta}\,d\theta = \int \sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln\left|\sec\theta + \tan\theta\right| + C_1

From the reference triangle, \tan\theta = \frac{x}{a} and \sec\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}}{a}, so

= \ln\left|\frac{x + \sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}}{a}\right| + C_1 = \ln\left|x + \sqrt{x^{2}+a^{2}}\right| + C

because -\ln a is itself a constant and is absorbed into C.

Any quadratic can be pushed into one of these forms by completing the square: ax^{2}+bx+c = a\left[\left(x+\frac{b}{2a}\right)^{2} + \frac{4ac-b^{2}}{4a^{2}}\right]. Then substitute t = x + \frac{b}{2a}.

Worked example 13.13

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int \frac{dx}{4x^{2}+9}, (b) \int \frac{dx}{x^{2}-16}, (c) \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{9-4x^{2}}}.

Solution. Force each into the shape x^{2} \pm a^{2} by taking the leading coefficient outside.

(a) 4x^{2}+9 = 4\left(x^{2} + \frac94\right), so a = \frac32:

\int \frac{dx}{4\left(x^{2}+\left(\frac32\right)^{2}\right)} = \frac14 \cdot \frac{1}{3/2}\tan^{-1}\frac{x}{3/2} + C = \frac{1}{6}\tan^{-1}\frac{2x}{3} + C

(b) Here a = 4 directly:

\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}-4^{2}} = \frac{1}{2(4)}\ln\left|\frac{x-4}{x+4}\right| + C = \frac{1}{8}\ln\left|\frac{x-4}{x+4}\right| + C

(c) 9-4x^{2} = 4\left(\frac94 - x^{2}\right), so \sqrt{9-4x^{2}} = 2\sqrt{\left(\frac32\right)^{2}-x^{2}}:

\frac12\int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{\left(\frac32\right)^{2}-x^{2}}} = \frac12 \sin^{-1}\frac{x}{3/2} + C = \frac12\sin^{-1}\frac{2x}{3} + C

Worked example 13.14

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int \frac{dx}{x^{2}+6x+13}, (b) \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+4x+13}}, (c) \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{5-4x-x^{2}}}.

Solution. Complete the square in every case.

(a) x^{2}+6x+13 = (x+3)^{2} + 4 = (x+3)^{2} + 2^{2}. Put t = x+3, dt = dx:

\int \frac{dt}{t^{2}+2^{2}} = \frac12\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{2} + C = \frac12\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+3}{2}\right) + C

(b) x^{2}+4x+13 = (x+2)^{2} + 9 = (x+2)^{2} + 3^{2}. With t = x+2:

\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^{2}+3^{2}}} = \ln\left|t + \sqrt{t^{2}+9}\right| + C = \ln\left|x+2+\sqrt{x^{2}+4x+13}\right| + C

(c) Take out the minus sign first: 5-4x-x^{2} = 5 - \left(x^{2}+4x\right) = 5 + 4 - (x+2)^{2} = 3^{2} - (x+2)^{2}. With t = x+2:

\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{3^{2}-t^{2}}} = \sin^{-1}\frac{t}{3} + C = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x+2}{3}\right) + C

Look at the sign of the x^{2} term *before* completing the square

\sqrt{x^{2}+4x+13} leads to a logarithm; \sqrt{5-4x-x^{2}} leads to an inverse sine. The difference is only the sign of x^{2}, and it changes the whole answer. Write the bracket out fully rather than doing it in your head.

The forms \frac{px+q}{ax^{2}+bx+c} and \frac{px+q}{\sqrt{ax^{2}+bx+c}}

With an x in the numerator, split the numerator into a multiple of the derivative of the quadratic plus a constant:

px + q = \lambda\left(2ax + b\right) + \mu

Comparing coefficients, \lambda = \frac{p}{2a} and \mu = q - \frac{pb}{2a}. The \lambda piece is a \frac{g'}{g} pattern (a logarithm, or a square root); the \mu piece is one of the quadratic standard forms just done.

Worked example 13.15

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{2x+3}{x^{2}+4x+5}\,dx.

Solution. The derivative of x^{2}+4x+5 is 2x+4. Write

2x+3 = (2x+4) - 1

so the integral splits into two:

\int \frac{2x+4}{x^{2}+4x+5}\,dx - \int \frac{dx}{x^{2}+4x+5}

The first is \frac{g'}{g}, giving \ln\left|x^{2}+4x+5\right|; and since x^{2}+4x+5 = (x+2)^{2}+1 > 0 we may drop the modulus. For the second, t = x+2 gives \int \frac{dt}{t^{2}+1} = \tan^{-1}(x+2). Hence

\int \frac{2x+3}{x^{2}+4x+5}\,dx = \ln\left(x^{2}+4x+5\right) - \tan^{-1}(x+2) + C

Worked example 13.16

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}\,dx.

Solution. The derivative of x^{2}+2x+3 is 2x+2, so

x+2 = \frac12(2x+2) + 1

\int \frac{x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}\,dx = \frac12\int \frac{2x+2}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}\,dx + \int \frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}}

In the first integral put u = x^{2}+2x+3, du = (2x+2)dx:

\frac12\int \frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} = \frac12 \cdot 2\sqrt{u} = \sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}

For the second, x^{2}+2x+3 = (x+1)^{2}+2, so with t = x+1, \int\frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^{2}+2}} = \ln\left|t+\sqrt{t^{2}+2}\right|. Altogether

= \sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3} + \ln\left|x+1+\sqrt{x^{2}+2x+3}\right| + C

Always check by differentiating

Integration has a free self-check that differentiation does not: differentiate your answer and see whether you get the integrand back. It takes fifteen seconds and it catches sign slips, missing factors of \frac12, and wrong partial fraction constants. In the examination, if a question is worth five marks, spend one of your minutes on this check — a wrong answer with perfect method still loses most of the marks.

Trigonometric substitutions

When a radical cannot be removed by completing the square alone, replace x by a trigonometric function chosen to make the radical collapse by a Pythagorean identity. Draw the reference triangle so that you can change back at the end.

Radical Substitute Radical becomes Because
\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} x = a\sin\theta a\cos\theta 1-\sin^{2}\theta = \cos^{2}\theta
\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}} x = a\tan\theta a\sec\theta 1+\tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta
\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} x = a\sec\theta a\tan\theta \sec^{2}\theta-1 = \tan^{2}\theta

Worked example 13.17

Problem. Derive \int \sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + C.

Solution. Put x = a\sin\theta, so dx = a\cos\theta\,d\theta and \sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} = a\cos\theta.

\int \sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx = \int a\cos\theta \cdot a\cos\theta\,d\theta = a^{2}\int \cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta

Use \cos^{2}\theta = \frac{1+\cos 2\theta}{2}:

= \frac{a^{2}}{2}\int (1 + \cos 2\theta)\,d\theta = \frac{a^{2}}{2}\left(\theta + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{2}\right) + C = \frac{a^{2}}{2}\theta + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin\theta\cos\theta + C

From the first reference triangle, \theta = \sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}, \sin\theta = \frac{x}{a} and \cos\theta = \frac{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}{a}, so

= \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{x}{a}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}}{a} + C = \frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a} + C

Worked example 13.18

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{x^{2}\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}.

Solution. The radical is \sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} with a = 3, so put x = 3\sec\theta, dx = 3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta and \sqrt{x^{2}-9} = 3\tan\theta.

\int \frac{3\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta}{9\sec^{2}\theta \cdot 3\tan\theta} = \frac{1}{9}\int \frac{d\theta}{\sec\theta} = \frac19\int \cos\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\sin\theta}{9} + C

From the third reference triangle, the hypotenuse is x, the adjacent side is 3, and the opposite side is \sqrt{x^{2}-9}, so \sin\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{x}. Hence

\int \frac{dx}{x^{2}\sqrt{x^{2}-9}} = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}{9x} + C

Check. Differentiating \frac{1}{9}\left(1 - \frac{9}{x^{2}}\right)^{1/2}, written this way to make the algebra short, returns \frac{1}{x^{2}\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}. Correct.

Worked example 13.19

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{x\sqrt{1+x^{2}}} by the inverse substitution x = \frac{1}{t}.

Solution. When a single power of x sits outside a heavy radical, the substitution x = \frac1t turns the radical inside out. Here dx = -\frac{dt}{t^{2}} and

\sqrt{1+x^{2}} = \sqrt{1 + \frac{1}{t^{2}}} = \frac{\sqrt{t^{2}+1}}{|t|}

Taking t>0 (i.e. x>0),

\int \frac{-dt/t^{2}}{\frac1t \cdot \frac{\sqrt{t^{2}+1}}{t}} = -\int \frac{dt}{\sqrt{t^{2}+1}} = -\ln\left|t + \sqrt{t^{2}+1}\right| + C

Putting t = \frac1x back,

= -\ln\left|\frac{1}{x} + \frac{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}{x}\right| + C = -\ln\left|\frac{1+\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}{x}\right| + C

The forms \frac{1}{a+b\cos x} and \frac{1}{a\sin x + b\cos x}

The half-angle (Weierstrass) substitution

Put t = \tan\dfrac{x}{2}. Then

\sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^{2}}, \qquad \cos x = \frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}, \qquad \tan x = \frac{2t}{1-t^{2}}, \qquad dx = \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}

Every rational function of \sin x and \cos x becomes a rational function of t, which §13.3 can always finish. To see where dx comes from: t=\tan\frac x2 gives \frac{dt}{dx} = \frac12\sec^{2}\frac{x}{2} = \frac{1+t^{2}}{2}.

Worked example 13.20

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{5+4\cos x}.

Solution. Put t = \tan\frac{x}{2}. Then

5 + 4\cos x = 5 + \frac{4\left(1-t^{2}\right)}{1+t^{2}} = \frac{5+5t^{2}+4-4t^{2}}{1+t^{2}} = \frac{9+t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}

and dx = \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}, so the factor 1+t^{2} cancels completely:

\int \frac{dx}{5+4\cos x} = \int \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}\cdot\frac{1+t^{2}}{9+t^{2}} = 2\int \frac{dt}{t^{2}+3^{2}}

= 2 \cdot \frac13\tan^{-1}\frac{t}{3} + C = \frac{2}{3}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{3}\tan\frac{x}{2}\right) + C

Worked example 13.21

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{3\sin x + 4\cos x}.

Solution. Again put t = \tan\frac{x}{2}:

3\sin x + 4\cos x = \frac{6t}{1+t^{2}} + \frac{4\left(1-t^{2}\right)}{1+t^{2}} = \frac{-4t^{2}+6t+4}{1+t^{2}}

\int \frac{dx}{3\sin x+4\cos x} = \int \frac{2\,dt}{-4t^{2}+6t+4} = -\int \frac{dt}{2t^{2}-3t-2} = -\int \frac{dt}{(2t+1)(t-2)}

Split by partial fractions. Writing \frac{1}{(2t+1)(t-2)} = \frac{A}{2t+1} + \frac{B}{t-2} gives 1 = A(t-2) + B(2t+1). Put t=2: 1 = 5B, so B = \frac15. Put t = -\frac12: 1 = -\frac52 A, so A = -\frac25. Hence

-\int \left[\frac{-2/5}{2t+1} + \frac{1/5}{t-2}\right]dt = \frac{1}{5}\ln|2t+1| - \frac{1}{5}\ln|t-2| + C

= \frac{1}{5}\ln\left|\frac{2\tan\frac{x}{2}+1}{\tan\frac{x}{2}-2}\right| + C

Notice the coefficient \frac15 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3^{2}+4^{2}}}. That is no accident: a\sin x + b\cos x = \sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}\,\sin(x+\alpha), so the integral always carries a factor \frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}+b^{2}}} — a fast way to check your answer.

13.3 Integrals of rational functions

A rational function is a quotient \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} of two polynomials. If \deg P \ge \deg Q the fraction is improper: divide first, so that

\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)} = \text{polynomial} + \frac{\text{remainder}}{Q(x)}

Once the fraction is proper, factorise Q(x) and split it into partial fractions. There are exactly four cases, decided entirely by the factors of the denominator.

The four partial-fraction cases
Factor of Q(x) Contributes
distinct linear (x-a) \dfrac{A}{x-a}
repeated linear (x-a)^{2} \dfrac{A}{x-a} + \dfrac{B}{(x-a)^{2}}
distinct irreducible quadratic (x^{2}+px+q) \dfrac{Ax+B}{x^{2}+px+q}
repeated quadratic (x^{2}+px+q)^{2} \dfrac{Ax+B}{x^{2}+px+q} + \dfrac{Cx+D}{(x^{2}+px+q)^{2}}

The number of unknown constants always equals \deg Q. Find them either by substituting convenient values of x (fastest for linear factors) or by comparing coefficients (necessary for quadratic factors).

Worked example 13.22

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x+2)} — distinct linear factors.

Solution. Write

\frac{1}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x+2}

Multiply through by (x-1)(x+2): \quad 1 = A(x+2) + B(x-1).

Put x = 1: \;1 = 3A, so A = \frac13. Put x = -2: \;1 = -3B, so B = -\frac13. Therefore

\int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x+2)} = \frac13\int\frac{dx}{x-1} - \frac13\int\frac{dx}{x+2}

= \frac13\ln|x-1| - \frac13\ln|x+2| + C = \frac{1}{3}\ln\left|\frac{x-1}{x+2}\right| + C

Worked example 13.23

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)} and \int \frac{x\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)}.

Solution. (a) With \frac{1}{(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)} = \frac{A}{x-1}+\frac{B}{x-2}+\frac{C}{x-3} we get 1 = A(x-2)(x-3) + B(x-1)(x-3) + C(x-1)(x-2).

Put x=1: 1 = A(-1)(-2) = 2A, so A = \frac12. Put x=2: 1 = B(1)(-1) = -B, so B = -1. Put x=3: 1 = C(2)(1) = 2C, so C = \frac12.

\int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)} = \frac12\ln|x-1| - \ln|x-2| + \frac12\ln|x-3| + C

(b) \frac{x}{(x-1)(x-2)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{x-2} gives x = A(x-2)+B(x-1). Put x=1: A = -1. Put x=2: B = 2. So

\int \frac{x\,dx}{(x-1)(x-2)} = -\ln|x-1| + 2\ln|x-2| + C

Worked example 13.24

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{3x+5}{(x-1)^{2}(x+1)}\,dx — a repeated linear factor.

Solution. The repeated factor needs two terms:

\frac{3x+5}{(x-1)^{2}(x+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{B}{(x-1)^{2}} + \frac{D}{x+1}

Multiplying by (x-1)^{2}(x+1):

3x+5 = A(x-1)(x+1) + B(x+1) + D(x-1)^{2}

Put x=1: \;8 = 2B, so B = 4. Put x=-1: \;2 = 4D, so D = \frac12. Compare the coefficients of x^{2}: \;0 = A + D, so A = -\frac12.

\int \frac{3x+5}{(x-1)^{2}(x+1)}dx = -\frac12\int\frac{dx}{x-1} + 4\int\frac{dx}{(x-1)^{2}} + \frac12\int\frac{dx}{x+1}

= -\frac12\ln|x-1| - \frac{4}{x-1} + \frac12\ln|x+1| + C

using \int (x-1)^{-2}dx = -\frac{1}{x-1}. Note that only the first-power terms give logarithms.

The repeated factor needs both powers

Writing only \frac{A}{(x-1)^{2}} + \frac{D}{x+1} gives two equations for a problem that needs three constants, and the identity then fails for general x. A factor (x-a)^{n} always contributes n terms, with denominators (x-a), (x-a)^{2}, \dots, (x-a)^{n}.

Worked example 13.25

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{(x-1)\left(x^{2}+1\right)} — an irreducible quadratic factor.

Solution. Since x^{2}+1 has no real factors, it takes a linear numerator:

\frac{1}{(x-1)(x^{2}+1)} = \frac{A}{x-1} + \frac{Bx+D}{x^{2}+1}

1 = A\left(x^{2}+1\right) + (Bx+D)(x-1)

Put x=1: \;1 = 2A, so A = \frac12. Coefficient of x^{2}: \;0 = A + B, so B = -\frac12. Constant term: \;1 = A - D, so D = -\frac12.

\int \frac{dx}{(x-1)(x^{2}+1)} = \frac12\int \frac{dx}{x-1} - \frac12\int \frac{x+1}{x^{2}+1}\,dx

Split the second integral: \frac{x}{x^{2}+1} is a \frac{g'}{2g} pattern and \frac{1}{x^{2}+1} is a standard form.

= \frac12\ln|x-1| - \frac14\ln\left(x^{2}+1\right) - \frac12\tan^{-1}x + C

Worked example 13.26

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{x^{3}+2x+1}{\left(x^{2}+1\right)^{2}}\,dx — a repeated quadratic factor.

Solution. The decomposition is

\frac{x^{3}+2x+1}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}} = \frac{Ax+B}{x^{2}+1} + \frac{Dx+E}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}

Multiplying up, \;x^{3}+2x+1 = (Ax+B)\left(x^{2}+1\right) + Dx + E, i.e.

x^{3}+2x+1 = Ax^{3} + Bx^{2} + (A+D)x + (B+E)

Comparing coefficients: A = 1, B = 0, A + D = 2 so D = 1, and B + E = 1 so E = 1. Hence

I = \int \frac{x\,dx}{x^{2}+1} + \int \frac{x\,dx}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}} + \int \frac{dx}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}}

The first two use u = x^{2}+1, du = 2x\,dx:

\int \frac{x\,dx}{x^{2}+1} = \frac12\ln\left(x^{2}+1\right), \qquad \int \frac{x\,dx}{(x^{2}+1)^{2}} = \frac12\int u^{-2}du = -\frac{1}{2(x^{2}+1)}

The third needs x = \tan\theta, dx = \sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta:

\int \frac{\sec^{2}\theta\,d\theta}{\sec^{4}\theta} = \int \cos^{2}\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin 2\theta}{4} = \frac{\theta}{2} + \frac{\sin\theta\cos\theta}{2}

With \theta = \tan^{-1}x, \sin\theta = \frac{x}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}} and \cos\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+x^{2}}}, this is \frac12\tan^{-1}x + \frac{x}{2\left(1+x^{2}\right)}. Collecting everything,

I = \frac12\ln\left(x^{2}+1\right) + \frac{x-1}{2\left(x^{2}+1\right)} + \frac12\tan^{-1}x + C

Worked example 13.27

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{x^{2}+1}{(x+1)(x+2)}\,dx and \int \frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1}\,dx — improper fractions.

Solution. In both, the numerator degree is not less than the denominator degree, so divide first.

(a) \frac{x^{2}+1}{x^{2}+3x+2} = 1 + \frac{-3x-1}{(x+1)(x+2)}. Now \frac{-3x-1}{(x+1)(x+2)} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{B}{x+2} gives -3x-1 = A(x+2)+B(x+1). Put x=-1: 2 = A. Put x=-2: 5 = -B, so B=-5.

\int \frac{x^{2}+1}{(x+1)(x+2)}dx = x + 2\ln|x+1| - 5\ln|x+2| + C

(b) \frac{x^{2}}{x^{2}+1} = 1 - \frac{1}{x^{2}+1}, so the integral is x - \tan^{-1}x + C at once. Dividing out first turns a hard-looking problem into a one-line one.

Worked example 13.28

Problem. Evaluate \int \frac{dx}{x^{3}+1}.

Solution. Factorise the denominator using a^{3}+b^{3} = (a+b)\left(a^{2}-ab+b^{2}\right): \;x^{3}+1 = (x+1)\left(x^{2}-x+1\right), and x^{2}-x+1 is irreducible (discriminant 1-4 = -3 < 0). So

\frac{1}{(x+1)(x^{2}-x+1)} = \frac{A}{x+1} + \frac{Bx+D}{x^{2}-x+1}

1 = A\left(x^{2}-x+1\right) + (Bx+D)(x+1)

Put x=-1: \;1 = 3A, so A = \frac13. Coefficient of x^{2}: 0 = A + B, so B = -\frac13. Constant: 1 = A + D, so D = \frac23. Then

I = \frac13\int\frac{dx}{x+1} - \frac13\int \frac{x-2}{x^{2}-x+1}\,dx

For the second integral, split the numerator using (x^{2}-x+1)' = 2x-1: \;x-2 = \frac12(2x-1) - \frac32. Also x^{2}-x+1 = \left(x-\frac12\right)^{2} + \frac34, so

\int \frac{x-2}{x^{2}-x+1}dx = \frac12\ln\left(x^{2}-x+1\right) - \frac32 \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{3}}

Therefore

\int \frac{dx}{x^{3}+1} = \frac13\ln|x+1| - \frac16\ln\left(x^{2}-x+1\right) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{2x-1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) + C

13.4 The definite integral and its properties

Everything so far produced a family of functions. A definite integral produces a single number, and that number measures an accumulation: area, distance, total charge, total cost.

The shift is worth dwelling on. If v(t) is the velocity of a bus on the Prithvi Highway, then \int v(t)\,dt is a family of position functions — useless until you know where the bus started. But \int_{9}^{12} v(t)\,dt is the distance covered between nine and twelve o'clock, and that is a definite number you can quote in kilometres. Definite integration is how a rate becomes a total.

Definite integral

If f is continuous on [a,b] and F is any anti-derivative of f, then

\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \left[F(x)\right]_{a}^{b} = F(b) - F(a)

Here a is the lower limit and b the upper limit. The constant of integration cancels, since \left(F(b)+C\right) - \left(F(a)+C\right) = F(b)-F(a), which is why a definite integral never carries +C.

The link between the two halves of calculus is the fundamental theorem: if A(x) = \int_{a}^{x} f(t)\,dt is the accumulated area up to x, then A'(x) = f(x). Differentiating an area function gives back the curve. The picture below is worth memorising, because it is the whole of calculus in two panels.

A definite integral counts area below the axis as negative. So \int_{a}^{b} f\,dx is a signed area, and it can be zero even when the region is large.

Worked example 13.29

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int_{1}^{2}\left(x^{2}+1\right)dx, (b) \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx, (c) \int_{0}^{3\pi/2}\sin x\,dx, (d) \int_{0}^{2\pi}\sin x\,dx.

Solution. Find an anti-derivative, then subtract.

(a) \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x\right]_{1}^{2} = \left(\frac83+2\right) - \left(\frac13+1\right) = \frac{14}{3} - \frac43 = \frac{10}{3}

(b) \left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = -\cos\pi + \cos 0 = 1+1 = 2

(c) \left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{3\pi/2} = -\cos\frac{3\pi}{2} + \cos 0 = 0 + 1 = 1

(d) \left[-\cos x\right]_{0}^{2\pi} = -1+1 = 0

Parts (b), (c) and (d) are the three cases drawn in the figure: all area above, part below, and exact cancellation.

Change the limits when you change the variable

In a definite integral you may either (i) convert the limits to the new variable, or (ii) integrate back to x first and then substitute. What you must never do is use the old limits with the new variable. In \int_{0}^{4}\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+9}} with u = x^{2}+9, the limits become u = 9 and u = 25, not 0 and 4.

Worked example 13.30

Problem. Evaluate \int_{0}^{4}\frac{x}{\sqrt{x^{2}+9}}\,dx and \int_{0}^{1} x e^{x}\,dx.

Solution. (a) Put u = x^{2}+9, so du = 2x\,dx. When x=0, u=9; when x=4, u=25.

\int_{0}^{4}\frac{x\,dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}+9}} = \frac12\int_{9}^{25}\frac{du}{\sqrt{u}} = \frac12\left[2\sqrt{u}\right]_{9}^{25} = \left[\sqrt{u}\right]_{9}^{25} = 5-3 = 2

(b) By parts, using Worked example 13.9:

\int_{0}^{1}x e^{x}dx = \left[(x-1)e^{x}\right]_{0}^{1} = (0)e^{1} - (-1)e^{0} = 0 + 1 = 1

The eight properties

Properties of the definite integral

P1 \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = -\int_{b}^{a} f(x)\,dx, and \displaystyle\int_{a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 0

P2 \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{c} f(x)\,dx + \int_{c}^{b} f(x)\,dx for any c

P3 \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(t)\,dt — the variable of integration is a dummy

P4 \displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-x)\,dx

P5 \displaystyle\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(a+b-x)\,dx

P6 \displaystyle\int_{-a}^{a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx if f is even, and = 0 if f is odd

P7 \displaystyle\int_{0}^{2a} f(x)\,dx = 2\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx if f(2a-x) = f(x), and = 0 if f(2a-x) = -f(x)

P8 \displaystyle\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx \ge 0 if f(x)\ge 0 on [a,b], and \left|\int_{a}^{b}f\right| \le \int_{a}^{b}|f|

Why P4 is true

In \int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx put x = a - t, so dx = -dt. When x=0, t=a, and when x=a, t=0:

\int_{0}^{a} f(x)\,dx = \int_{a}^{0} f(a-t)\,(-dt) = \int_{0}^{a} f(a-t)\,dt

using P1 to swap the limits and absorb the minus sign. By P3 the dummy t may be renamed x, which is P4. The same substitution x = a+b-t proves P5.

P4 and P5 are the two properties that make "impossible" integrals collapse: add the original to the reflected copy and the integrand often becomes a constant.

Worked example 13.31

Problem. Evaluate I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\pi/2} \frac{\sqrt{\sin x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}}\,dx.

Solution. No anti-derivative of this integrand exists in elementary terms, so use P4 with a = \frac{\pi}{2}. Since \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \cos x and \cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right) = \sin x,

I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sqrt{\cos x}+\sqrt{\sin x}}\,dx

Add the two expressions for I. The denominators are now identical:

2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}}{\sqrt{\sin x}+\sqrt{\cos x}}\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2} 1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}

I = \frac{\pi}{4}

The same argument gives \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\tan x} = \frac{\pi}{4} and \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}x\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}x\,dx = \frac{\pi}{4}, because in each case the two copies add to 1.

Worked example 13.32

Problem. Use P6 to evaluate \int_{-1}^{1}\left(x^{3}+x\right)dx and \int_{-2}^{2}x^{2}\,dx.

Solution. Test the parity first.

(a) f(-x) = -x^{3}-x = -f(x), so f is odd and the integral over a symmetric interval is 0. (Check directly: \left[\frac{x^{4}}{4}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{-1}^{1} = \frac34 - \frac34 = 0.)

(b) f(-x) = x^{2} = f(x), so f is even:

\int_{-2}^{2}x^{2}dx = 2\int_{0}^{2}x^{2}dx = 2\left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2 \cdot \frac83 = \frac{16}{3}

For a mixed integrand, split it: \int_{-2}^{2}\left(x^{3}+3x^{2}\right)dx = 0 + 3 \cdot \frac{16}{3} = 16, because the cube is odd and the square is even. Recognising parity turns a two-substitution problem into one line.

Worked example 13.33

Problem. Evaluate \int_{0}^{\pi} x\sin x\,dx two ways.

Solution. By parts. With u = x and dv = \sin x\,dx,

\int_{0}^{\pi}x\sin x\,dx = \left[-x\cos x\right]_{0}^{\pi} + \int_{0}^{\pi}\cos x\,dx = \pi + \left[\sin x\right]_{0}^{\pi} = \pi + 0 = \pi

By P4. Replacing x by \pi - x and using \sin(\pi-x) = \sin x,

I = \int_{0}^{\pi}(\pi-x)\sin x\,dx = \pi\int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx - I

so 2I = \pi \cdot 2 = 2\pi and I = \pi. The second method needs only \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\,dx = 2, and it generalises: for any f, \int_{0}^{\pi}x f(\sin x)\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}\int_{0}^{\pi}f(\sin x)\,dx.

Worked example 13.34

Problem. Evaluate (a) \int_{1}^{2}\frac{dx}{x(x+1)}, (b) \int_{3}^{5}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}}, (c) \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{3}x\,dx.

Solution. (a) Partial fractions: \frac{1}{x(x+1)} = \frac1x - \frac{1}{x+1}, so

\left[\ln|x| - \ln|x+1|\right]_{1}^{2} = \left[\ln\frac{x}{x+1}\right]_{1}^{2} = \ln\frac23 - \ln\frac12 = \ln\frac43

(b) A standard form with a=3:

\left[\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-9}\right|\right]_{3}^{5} = \ln(5+4) - \ln 3 = \ln 9 - \ln 3 = \ln 3

(c) Write \cos^{3}x = \cos x\left(1-\sin^{2}x\right) and put u = \sin x, with limits u=0 to u=1:

\int_{0}^{1}\left(1-u^{2}\right)du = \left[u - \frac{u^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = 1 - \frac13 = \frac{2}{3}

13.5 The definite integral as the limit of a sum

The definite integral was defined long before anti-derivatives, as the limiting total of thin rectangles. NEB asks for this derivation, so learn the four steps.

The idea is older than calculus: Greek mathematicians found areas by filling shapes with polygons and letting the number of sides grow. What Newton and Leibniz added was the discovery that this limit can be computed without any limits at all, by anti-differentiating. When a question says "evaluate as the limit of a sum", however, it is asking for the long method, and no marks are available for quoting F(b)-F(a).

The definite integral as a limit

Divide [a,b] into n equal sub-intervals, each of width h = \frac{b-a}{n}. The division points are a,\;a+h,\;a+2h,\;\dots,\;a+nh = b.

Step 1. On the r-th sub-interval take the rectangle of height f(a+rh) (the right-hand endpoint). Its area is h\,f(a+rh).

Step 2. Add the n rectangles:

S_{n} = h\sum_{r=1}^{n} f(a+rh) = \frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\left(a + \frac{r(b-a)}{n}\right)

Step 3. As n\to\infty the rectangles get thinner and S_{n} closes in on the exact area. Define

\int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\left(a + \frac{r(b-a)}{n}\right)

Step 4. Evaluate the sum in closed form using \sum r = \frac{n(n+1)}{2}, \sum r^{2} = \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}, \sum r^{3} = \frac{n^{2}(n+1)^{2}}{4}, or the geometric series for e^{x}, and then take the limit.

Worked example 13.35

Problem. Evaluate \int_{0}^{1}x^{2}\,dx as the limit of a sum.

Solution. Here a=0, b=1, f(x)=x^{2} and h = \frac1n, so f(a+rh) = \left(\frac{r}{n}\right)^{2}.

S_{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r^{2}}{n^{2}} = \frac{1}{n^{3}}\sum_{r=1}^{n} r^{2} = \frac{1}{n^{3}} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6}

Expand the numerator and divide through by n^{3}:

S_{n} = \frac{2n^{2}+3n+1}{6n^{2}} = \frac{1}{6}\left(2 + \frac{3}{n} + \frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)

Let n\to\infty, so that \frac3n\to 0 and \frac{1}{n^{2}}\to 0:

\int_{0}^{1}x^{2}dx = \lim_{n\to\infty} S_{n} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}

This agrees with \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac13, and the numbers in the figure — 0.4688, 0.3850, 0.3459 — are S_4, S_{10} and S_{40} from this very formula.

Worked example 13.36

Problem. Evaluate \int_{0}^{1}e^{x}\,dx and \int_{0}^{2}\left(x^{2}+1\right)dx as limits of sums.

Solution. (a) With h = \frac1n, f(a+rh) = e^{r/n}, so the sum is geometric with first term e^{1/n} and ratio e^{1/n}:

S_{n} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}e^{r/n} = \frac{1}{n} \cdot \frac{e^{1/n}\left(e^{n \cdot \frac1n}-1\right)}{e^{1/n}-1} = \frac{e^{1/n}(e-1)}{n\left(e^{1/n}-1\right)}

Write t = \frac1n, so t\to 0 as n\to\infty:

\lim_{n\to\infty}S_{n} = (e-1)\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{e^{t} \cdot t}{e^{t}-1} = (e-1) \cdot 1 = e-1

using the standard limit \lim_{t\to 0}\frac{e^{t}-1}{t} = 1. And indeed \left[e^{x}\right]_{0}^{1} = e-1.

(b) Now a=0, b=2, h = \frac2n and f(a+rh) = \frac{4r^{2}}{n^{2}}+1:

S_{n} = \frac{2}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{4r^{2}}{n^{2}}+1\right) = \frac{8}{n^{3}} \cdot \frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \frac{2}{n} \cdot n

= \frac{4}{3}\left(2+\frac3n+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right)\cdot\frac12 \cdot 2 + 2 \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{8}{3} + 2 = \frac{14}{3}

which matches \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+x\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac83+2 = \frac{14}{3}.

13.6 Area under a curve and area between two curves

The four area formulas

Under a curve, above the x-axis:

A = \int_{a}^{b} y\,dx = \int_{a}^{b} f(x)\,dx

Between a curve and the y-axis (horizontal strips):

A = \int_{c}^{d} x\,dy

Between two curves, with f the upper one on [a,b]:

A = \int_{a}^{b}\left[f(x) - g(x)\right]dx

When the curve dips below the axis, integrate each piece separately and add the absolute values, because area is never negative.

The strip is the thing to picture. A vertical strip at x has height y and thickness dx, so its area is y\,dx, and the integral sweeps it from a to b. A horizontal strip at height y has length x and thickness dy, giving x\,dy.

Every area question is then the same four steps.

  1. Sketch the curves, roughly but with the intersections and axis crossings in the right places.
  2. Find the limits by solving the two equations simultaneously, or by setting y=0 if one boundary is the axis.
  3. Decide the strip direction, and which boundary is the upper or outer one.
  4. Integrate the strip area and evaluate.

Skipping the sketch is what causes the two classic errors: subtracting the curves the wrong way round, and missing a region where the curve crosses the axis.

Worked example 13.37

Problem. Find the area bounded by y = x^{2}, the x-axis and the lines x=0 and x=3.

Solution. The curve is above the axis throughout [0,3], so

A = \int_{0}^{3} x^{2}\,dx = \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{3} = \frac{27}{3} - 0 = 9 \text{ square units}

Similarly \int_{0}^{2}x^{3}dx = \left[\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{2} = 4 and \int_{1}^{e}\frac{dx}{x} = \left[\ln x\right]_{1}^{e} = 1 — the area under the rectangular hyperbola from 1 to e is exactly one square unit, which is what makes e the natural base.

Worked example 13.38

Problem. Find the area enclosed between the line y = 2x and the parabola y = x^{2}.

Solution. Step 1 — find the intersections. Solve x^{2} = 2x, i.e. x(x-2) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 2.

Step 2 — decide which curve is on top. At x=1, the line gives 2 and the parabola gives 1, so the line is above throughout (0,2).

Step 3 — integrate the difference.

A = \int_{0}^{2}\left(2x - x^{2}\right)dx = \left[x^{2} - \frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 4 - \frac83 = \frac{4}{3}

Step 4 — state the answer. The enclosed area is \frac43 square units.

Worked example 13.39

Problem. Find the area bounded by the parabola x = y^{2}, the y-axis and the line y = 2.

Solution. The bounding line is horizontal and the region touches the y-axis, so use horizontal strips and integrate with respect to y. A strip at height y has length x = y^{2} and thickness dy, so

A = \int_{0}^{2} x\,dy = \int_{0}^{2} y^{2}\,dy = \left[\frac{y^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{8}{3}\text{ square units}

Doing the same region with vertical strips would need \int_{0}^{4}\left(2-\sqrt{x}\right)dx — correct, but longer. Choose the strip direction that makes the limits constants.

Worked example 13.40

Problem. Find the area of the circle x^{2}+y^{2} = a^{2}, and hence the area of the ellipse \frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1.

Solution. Circle. By symmetry the total area is four times the first quadrant piece, where y = \sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} and x runs from 0 to a:

A = 4\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx = 4\left[\frac{x}{2}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}} + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\sin^{-1}\frac{x}{a}\right]_{0}^{a}

using Worked example 13.17. At x=a the first term vanishes and \sin^{-1}1 = \frac{\pi}{2}, so

A = 4\left(0 + \frac{a^{2}}{2}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}\right) = \pi a^{2}

Ellipse. In the first quadrant y = \frac{b}{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}, so the whole calculation is scaled by \frac ba:

A = 4\cdot\frac{b}{a}\int_{0}^{a}\sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}\,dx = \frac{4b}{a}\cdot\frac{\pi a^{2}}{4} = \pi a b

With a=4 and b=3 this gives 12\pi, and the shaded quarter in the figure is 3\pi.

Worked example 13.41

Problem. Find the area enclosed between the parabolas y^{2} = 4x and x^{2} = 4y.

Solution. Intersections. From the second, y = \frac{x^{2}}{4}. Substituting into the first, \frac{x^{4}}{16} = 4x, so x^{4} = 64x, giving x\left(x^{3}-64\right) = 0 and hence x = 0 or x = 4.

Upper curve. At x=1, y^{2}=4x gives y = 2 while x^{2}=4y gives y = \frac14. So y = 2\sqrt{x} is above y = \frac{x^{2}}{4}.

A = \int_{0}^{4}\left(2\sqrt{x} - \frac{x^{2}}{4}\right)dx = \left[\frac{4x^{3/2}}{3} - \frac{x^{3}}{12}\right]_{0}^{4}

= \frac{4 \cdot 8}{3} - \frac{64}{12} = \frac{32}{3} - \frac{16}{3} = \frac{16}{3}\text{ square units}

Worked example 13.42

Problem. Find the area bounded by y = 4-x^{2} and the x-axis, and the area enclosed between y = x^{2} and y = x^{3}.

Solution. (a) The parabola cuts the axis where 4-x^{2}=0, i.e. x = \pm 2, and is above the axis between them. The function is even, so

A = 2\int_{0}^{2}\left(4-x^{2}\right)dx = 2\left[4x - \frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = 2\left(8-\frac83\right) = \frac{32}{3}

(b) x^{2} = x^{3} gives x^{2}(1-x) = 0, so x = 0 and x = 1. On (0,1) we have x^{2} > x^{3} (test x = \frac12: \frac14 > \frac18), so

A = \int_{0}^{1}\left(x^{2}-x^{3}\right)dx = \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}-\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac13-\frac14 = \frac{1}{12}

Areas below the axis

\int_{-1}^{1}x^{3}dx = 0, but the region between the cubic and the axis from -1 to 1 has area \frac12. If the curve crosses the axis inside the interval, find the crossing points first, integrate over each piece, and add the magnitudes. Writing a single integral and reporting a negative "area" loses the mark every time.

Chapter summary

  • Anti-differentiation reverses differentiation: \int f(x)\,dx = F(x)+C where F' = f. The +C is compulsory, and it makes the answer a whole family of parallel curves.
  • Learn the table of standard integrals to the point of recall, including \int\frac{dx}{x} = \ln|x|, the nine quadratic forms, and \int\tan x\,dx = \ln|\sec x|, \int\sec x\,dx = \ln|\sec x+\tan x|.
  • Substitution works when the integrand contains g(x) together with g'(x). The master pattern is \int\frac{g'(x)}{g(x)}dx = \ln|g(x)|+C.
  • By parts: \int u\,dv = uv - \int v\,du, with u chosen by ILATE. Polynomial times sine or exponential needs repeated parts; e^{ax}\sin bx is cyclic, so apply parts twice and solve for I; and \int e^{x}\left[f+f'\right]dx = e^{x}f(x)+C in one step.
  • A quadratic denominator is handled by completing the square; an x in the numerator by splitting px+q = \lambda(\text{denominator})' + \mu.
  • Radicals \sqrt{a^{2}-x^{2}}, \sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}, \sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} call for x = a\sin\theta, a\tan\theta, a\sec\theta; draw the reference triangle to convert back.
  • Any rational function of \sin x and \cos x yields to t = \tan\frac{x}{2}, using \sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^{2}}, \cos x = \frac{1-t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}, dx = \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}.
  • Rational functions: divide first if improper, then split into partial fractions according to the four denominator cases.
  • \int_{a}^{b}f = F(b)-F(a) is a number and a signed area. The properties P4, P5 (reflection) and P6, P7 (symmetry) evaluate integrals whose anti-derivatives do not exist in elementary form.
  • As a limit of a sum, \int_{a}^{b}f\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n} f\left(a+\frac{r(b-a)}{n}\right).
  • Areas: \int_{a}^{b}y\,dx for vertical strips, \int_{c}^{d}x\,dy for horizontal strips, \int_{a}^{b}(\text{upper}-\text{lower})\,dx between two curves, and split the interval wherever the curve crosses the axis.

  1. Evaluate \int x^{2}\sin x\,dx. [5]

  4. Using the properties of definite integrals, evaluate \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\dfrac{dx}{1+\tan x}. [5]
  5. Evaluate \int \dfrac{dx}{1+\sin x} by the substitution t=\tan\dfrac{x}{2}. [5]

Answers to Group B

1. By ILATE take u=x^{2}, dv=\sin x\,dx, so v=-\cos x:

\int x^{2}\sin x\,dx = -x^{2}\cos x + 2\int x\cos x\,dx

Apply parts again with u=x, dv=\cos x\,dx, v=\sin x: \int x\cos x\,dx = x\sin x + \cos x. Hence

\int x^{2}\sin x\,dx = -x^{2}\cos x + 2x\sin x + 2\cos x + C

2. Complete the square: x^{2}+6x+13 = (x+3)^{2}+2^{2}. Put t = x+3, so dt = dx:

\int\frac{dt}{t^{2}+2^{2}} = \frac12\tan^{-1}\frac t2 + C = \frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x+3}{2}\right) + C

3. Let \frac{2x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)} = \frac{A}{x+1}+\frac{B}{x-2}, so 2x+1 = A(x-2)+B(x+1). Put x=-1: -1 = -3A, so A = \frac13. Put x=2: 5 = 3B, so B = \frac53. Therefore

\int\frac{2x+1}{(x+1)(x-2)}dx = \frac13\ln|x+1| + \frac53\ln|x-2| + C

4. Write I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{dx}{1+\tan x} = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos x\,dx}{\cos x+\sin x}. By P4, replacing x by \frac{\pi}{2}-x swaps \sin and \cos:

I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin x\,dx}{\sin x+\cos x}

Adding the two forms, 2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}, so I = \frac{\pi}{4}.

5. With t=\tan\frac x2 we have \sin x = \frac{2t}{1+t^{2}} and dx = \frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}, so

1+\sin x = \frac{1+t^{2}+2t}{1+t^{2}} = \frac{(1+t)^{2}}{1+t^{2}}

\int\frac{dx}{1+\sin x} = \int\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^{2}}\cdot\frac{1+t^{2}}{(1+t)^{2}} = 2\int\frac{dt}{(1+t)^{2}} = -\frac{2}{1+t} + C

= -\frac{2}{1+\tan\frac{x}{2}} + C

6. The curves meet where x = x^{3}, i.e. x\left(x^{2}-1\right)=0, so in the first quadrant x=0 and x=1. On (0,1), x > x^{3} (at x=\frac12, \frac12 > \frac18), so the line is above:

A = \int_{0}^{1}\left(x-x^{3}\right)dx = \left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}-\frac{x^{4}}{4}\right]_{0}^{1} = \frac12-\frac14 = \frac{1}{4}\text{ square units}

1. Put x = a\sec\theta. Then dx = a\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta and

\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}} = \sqrt{a^{2}\left(\sec^{2}\theta-1\right)} = a\tan\theta

so

\int\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}} = \int\frac{a\sec\theta\tan\theta\,d\theta}{a\tan\theta} = \int\sec\theta\,d\theta = \ln\left|\sec\theta+\tan\theta\right| + C_{1}

From the reference triangle, \sec\theta = \frac xa and \tan\theta = \frac{\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}}{a}, so

= \ln\left|\frac{x+\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}}{a}\right| + C_{1} = \ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-a^{2}}\right| + C

since -\ln a is absorbed into the constant. With a=3,

\int_{3}^{5}\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^{2}-9}} = \left[\ln\left|x+\sqrt{x^{2}-9}\right|\right]_{3}^{5} = \ln(5+4) - \ln 3 = \ln\frac93 = \ln 3

2. (a) Divide [a,b] into n equal parts of width h=\frac{b-a}{n} and define

\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\,dx = \lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{b-a}{n}\sum_{r=1}^{n}f\left(a+\frac{r(b-a)}{n}\right)

Here a=0, b=1, h=\frac1n and f\left(\frac rn\right) = \frac{r^{2}}{n^{2}}+\frac rn, so

S_{n} = \frac1n\sum_{r=1}^{n}\left(\frac{r^{2}}{n^{2}}+\frac{r}{n}\right) = \frac{1}{n^{3}}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{6} + \frac{1}{n^{2}}\cdot\frac{n(n+1)}{2}

= \frac{1}{6}\left(2+\frac3n+\frac{1}{n^{2}}\right) + \frac12\left(1+\frac1n\right)

Letting n\to\infty gives \frac{2}{6}+\frac12 = \frac13+\frac12 = \frac{5}{6}, which agrees with \left[\frac{x^{3}}{3}+\frac{x^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}.

(b) Substituting x = a-t in \int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx gives dx = -dt with limits reversed, so \int_{0}^{a}f(x)\,dx = \int_{0}^{a}f(a-t)\,dt, which is the stated property. Taking a=\frac{\pi}{2} and f(x)=\sin^{2}x, and using \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-x\right)=\cos x,

I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\sin^{2}x\,dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\cos^{2}x\,dx

Adding, 2I = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}\left(\sin^{2}x+\cos^{2}x\right)dx = \int_{0}^{\pi/2}1\,dx = \frac{\pi}{2}, so I = \frac{\pi}{4}.

3. (a) For y^{2}=8x we have 4a = 8, so a = 2 and the latus rectum is x = 2. The curve is symmetric about the x-axis, so the area is twice the part above it, where y = \sqrt{8x} = 2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{x}:

A = 2\int_{0}^{2}2\sqrt{2}\,\sqrt{x}\,dx = 4\sqrt{2}\left[\frac{2x^{3/2}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2} = \frac{8\sqrt{2}}{3}\cdot 2\sqrt{2} = \frac{32}{3}\text{ square units}

(b) The curves meet where x^{2} = x+2, i.e. x^{2}-x-2 = 0, giving (x-2)(x+1)=0, so x=-1 and x=2. Between them the line is above (at x=0 it gives 2 against 0), so

A = \int_{-1}^{2}\left(x+2-x^{2}\right)dx = \left[\frac{x^{2}}{2}+2x-\frac{x^{3}}{3}\right]_{-1}^{2}

= \left(2+4-\frac83\right) - \left(\frac12-2+\frac13\right) = \frac{10}{3} + \frac76 = \frac{27}{6} = \frac{9}{2}\text{ square units}
